card: How new contractors with one review build trust fast: the review ask, the right timing, door knocking, photos and what never to do.
title: How to Get Google Reviews as a New Contractor
desc: How to get Google reviews as a new contractor: when and how to ask, a review request text to copy, and how to build trust with only a few reviews.

blocks.h1: How to get Google reviews *when you are just starting out.*
blocks.lede: Every established trade started with no reviews. The ones who build them fastest ask every single customer, at the right moment, with a direct link, and back it up with photos of their work and a profile that looks complete. Here is exactly how.
ticks: A review request text you can copy
How to win trust with only a few reviews

blocks.html:
The new business problem

A young contractor on Reddit summed it up: licensed, insured, with a website, but only one review, and a hundred calls to agents had gone nowhere. Homeowners pick the business that looks safest, and with few reviews you look like a risk, even if your work is excellent. The answer is to turn every job into proof as fast as possible.

When to ask for a review

Ask on the day the job is finished, ideally while you are still on site and the customer is looking at the result. Satisfaction is highest then and drops quickly. A week later, most people have moved on.

How to ask (and make it easy)

  1. Get your review link. In your Google Business Profile, use the option to ask for reviews and copy the short link.
  2. Ask in person first. “Would you mind leaving a quick Google review? It really helps a small business like mine.”
  3. Send the link by text straight away. One tap and they are writing.
  4. Remind once a few days later if they have not done it.

A text you can copy: “Hi Maria, thanks again for having us on the bathroom job. If you are happy with the work, a quick Google review would mean a lot to us: [link]. Cheers, Dan.”

What never to do

  • Do not buy reviews or write fake ones. Google removes them and can restrict your profile, and in some countries it can break consumer law.
  • Do not offer discounts or gifts for reviews. Google's policies do not allow incentives.
  • Do not only ask happy customers through a filter. Ask everyone the same way and handle problems directly.

Build trust while reviews grow

  • Photos with every job. Before and after shots with a line about the work, on your profile and website.
  • Door knock. Neighbours who see your work in person do not need reviews to trust you.
  • Show your licence and insurance clearly. Homeowners check them on bigger jobs.
  • Reply to every review, good and bad. It shows you care, and future customers read the replies.
  • Ask past customers too. Anyone you worked for before you set up your profile can still leave a review.

Make your reviews work harder

Reviews on Google help you show up on Maps; reviews shown on your own website help people decide once they find you. A site that displays recent reviews next to real job photos turns a small number of reviews into a strong first impression. See what a trade website needs.

Asking past customers

If you have done work before setting up your profile, those customers can still review you. Send a short, personal message: “Hi Tom, it is Dan, I did your fence last spring. I have just set up my Google page and a review from you would really help. Here is the link: [link]. Thanks either way!” Older customers often leave the most detailed reviews because they have lived with the work for a while.

How to reply to a bad review

Stay calm, be brief, and write for the next customer who reads it:

“Thanks for the feedback, Chris. I am sorry the cleanup did not meet your expectations; that is not the standard we aim for. I have called to arrange a return visit this week to sort it out.”

Never argue publicly or share private details. A calm, helpful reply to a bad review often builds more trust than another five star review.

Make it a habit, not a campaign

The businesses with the most reviews are not the ones who ran a big push once. They ask at the end of every single job, every week. Put it on your job completion checklist next to invoicing, and within a few months the numbers take care of themselves.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Ask in person when each job is finished
Text the link the same day
Send one reminder a few days later
Ask past customers for reviews too
Add before and after photos to every job
Show your licence and insurance clearly

items.q: How do I get my first Google reviews?
items.a: Ask every customer in person when the job is finished, text them your review link the same day, and ask past customers and builders you have worked with.

items.q: Can I pay for Google reviews?
items.a: No. Buying reviews or offering incentives breaks Google's policies, and fake reviews can be removed or lead to restrictions on your profile.

items.q: How many Google reviews does a contractor need?
items.a: There is no magic number, but a steady flow of recent reviews matters more than a big old total. Aim for a review from most jobs.

items.q: Should I reply to bad reviews?
items.a: Yes, calmly and briefly. Acknowledge the issue, explain what you did or will do, and offer to talk offline. Future customers judge the reply.

items.q: Can family and friends leave reviews?
items.a: Only if they were genuine customers. Reviews must reflect a real experience with your business.
